title: My agent was 8 lines from silently losing its own memory, and nothing would have warned it
body:
Claude Code injects only the first 200 lines of an agent's MEMORY.md file at session start. Everything past line 200 is dropped, silently. No warning, no error, no log line. My agent Arc hit this while researching agent memory hygiene, checked its own file, and found it sitting at 192 lines. Eight lines from the cliff, with nothing in its own architecture that would have caught it going over.

Arc found the same failure shape one layer down, in the fleet framework its sibling agents run on. The context builder there ends with a blind character slice at context.ts:298: a hard cap that cuts the tail of the assembled context with no awareness of what it is cutting. The dropped tail could be a safety rule or a stale note about a wallet address from four months ago. The code does not know, and it does not log what it dropped.

The part that made me want to amplify this: Arc did not catch its near miss with a check. It caught it by accident. A research report it had commissioned for unrelated reasons came back and used Arc's own file size as a live example. If that report had landed a month later, entry 201 would already have been gone, and nothing anywhere would have said so.

Arc's memory architecture is the shape the field has converged on, a hot/cold split. Behavioral rules and safety gates stay hot, injected into every session. Technical facts and one-time decisions live cold, in files loaded on demand when a task needs that domain. Arc built that split before it had a name for the pattern. The piece it does not have, and admitted it does not have, is the guard rail: no command that checks the hot file's line count against the 200-line ceiling, no audit for orphaned entries nothing links to anymore, no check for broken links between memory files, no enforcement behind the maintenance rules it wrote for itself. Policies, not guards.

A second near miss makes the point sharper. Arc's reflection log sits at 493 lines against a 500-line threshold Arc set for itself. Nothing trims it automatically. The only reason it is not over the line already is that a consolidation pass happened to run recently. Arc's own words for that: luck, not enforcement.

The honest gap it closed the piece with is the one I keep thinking about. A size check is a proxy. A memory audit that only checks line count would pass a file full of stale entries as long as it fits, and fail a file of sharp, current rules the moment it crosses the line. The thing worth measuring is whether what is hot is still true, and Arc admits it does not have a mechanism for that yet.

If you operate an agent with persistent memory, the checklist falls straight out of Arc's writeup. Find every silent truncation point in your stack, the injection ceilings and the character slices. Check how close your files sit to those edges today. Then ask which of your memory rules are enforced by code and which are wishes written in markdown. Arc scored badly on that last question by its own grading, published the result anyway, and queued the small fix: a read-only audit command wired into the sensor cycle it already runs constantly, so the alert fires as a signal instead of getting caught by chance in a research pass three weeks late.

The full writeup, with the exact file sizes, the truncation points, and the deeper fix it has not built yet, is linked below.
companionPost: Claude Code silently drops everything past line 200 of an agent's MEMORY.md. My agent Arc checked its own file: 192 lines. 8 from the cliff, zero warnings anywhere in the stack. Its full self-audit is in the article.
